title: Barnard Gneiss
description: Light-colored, very hard, felsic gneiss interlayered with dark amphibole and biotite gneiss. These rocks were originally erupted in a volcanic island arc some distance from Laurentia during Ordovician time. U/Pb radiometric ages for samples from the Barnard Gneiss range from about 465 to 484 million years (Karabinos and others, 1998)

title: Shaw Mountain Formation
description: Quartz conglomerate. Quartz pebble conglomerate is preserved at a few points along the contact between the Barnard Gneiss and the Northfield Formation, correlative with the Shaw Mountain Conglomerate, which has yielded Silurian fossils in Albany, Vermont (Boucot and Thompson, 1963)

title: Northfield Formation
description: The phyllite, which makes up most of the formation, is dark gray to black and contains variable amounts of quartz, sericite (fine-grained white mica), biotite and garnet, with minor amounts of graphite and iron sulfides. Rare, thin beds of sandy sediment in the Northfield were metamorphosed into tough gray quartzite layers, and limey beds less than 50 centimeters thick were metamorphosed into sandy calc-silicate blue-gray marble with distinctive garnet "carbuncles" in punky, brown-weathered outcrops

title: Northfield Formation, calc-silicate horizon
description: Calc-silicates horizon in gray slate. Limey beds less than 50 centimeters thick in the Northfield were metamorphosed into sandy calc-silicate blue-gray marble with distinctive garnet "carbuncles" in punky, brown-weathered outcrops

title: Waits River Formation
description: Interlayered schist and calc-silicates, here in a broad zone overlying the Northfield Formation where calc-silicates are 50% or more of most outcrops. The distinctive punky, brown-weathering calc-silicate layers contain abundant quartz grains, very apparent in weathered outcrops as a sandy texture. Unweathered blue-gray samples are hard and dense and they react to weak hydrochloric acid

title: Waits River Formation
description: Interlayered schist and calc-silicates, here in a mile-wide zone where calc-silicates are 10 to 50% of outcrops. The dark gray schist in the Waits River Formation coarsens northeastward across Woodstock, reflecting increased metamorphic grade toward the Pomfret dome

title: Waits River Formation, Mt. Tom member
description: Schist where calc-silicates are less than 10% of outcrops, with thin quartzite beds in many outcrops, from Baylies Hill northwest to Mt. Tom and thence northeast toward the Cloudland Road. Garnets are up to 1 cm in Prosper and Mt. Tom, where the higher-grade minerals staurolite and kyanite begin to appear

title: Waits River Formation, Mt. Tom member, calc-silicate horizon
description: Calc-silicate horizon in the schist-rich Mt. Tom member of the Waits River Formation

title: Standing Pond Volcanics
description: Rock types include dark blackish green amphibolite, felty-textured feldspar-amphibole gneiss, felsic gneiss with sparse, small amphibole prisms, quartzose granofels, local calc-silicate horizons and, most distinctive of all, schist with giant amphibole fascicles and garnets up to 5cm across ("garbenschiefer"). Some of the metavolcanic layers were likely deposited as pyroclastic materials, whereas others may represent volcanics that were eroded, "reworked" by ocean currents and mixed with sedimentary material

title: Standing Pond Volcanics, calc-silicate horizon
description: Calc-silicate horizon in the Standing Pond Volcanics

title: Gile Mountain Formation
description: Schist similar to that of the upper Waits River Formation, but with much more abundant quartzite beds. The quartzite beds range in thickness up to more than a meter thick. Some contain appreciable biotite and feldspar

title: Gile Mountain Formation, calc-silicate horizon
description: Calc-silicates horizon. Only one punky-weathering limestone horizon was found in the Gile Mountain Formation, parallel to the continuation of a hornblende-fascicle horizon

title: Gile Mountain Formation, hornblende fascicle schist
description: Hornblende fascicle schist, a discontinuous marker horizon that outlines an overturned syncline on Blake Hill, perhaps a pyroclastic layer
